summaries.example: Imagine pushing a box. If your push is stronger than the box’s resistance, the box moves. Kilvington used this kind of comparison to think about motion. He also used imaginary cases, such as motion in an empty space, to test whether an explanation made sense.
summaries.summary: Richard Kilvington was an Oxford scholar who lived in the 1300s. He worked in several areas that we now call philosophy: logic, the study of nature, ethics, and theology. He was one of the early Oxford Calculators, a group known for using mathematical ideas to study change and motion. Kilvington asked what happens when a force is greater than resistance, how speed can be measured, and whether a continuous thing such as a line has infinitely many parts. He also used imaginary cases. These were thought experiments: situations made up to discover whether a rule led to a contradiction. In ethics, he argued that repeated actions can strengthen or weaken virtues and that experience is needed for wise decisions. In theology, he discussed God’s power, knowledge, human freedom, and future events within the religious ideas of his time. His methods and arguments influenced later scholars in England and elsewhere.
key_ideas: Richard Kilvington was a fourteenth-century scholar connected with Oxford. He studied logic, nature, ethics, and theology.
He believed that logic and mathematics could help explain both real events and carefully imagined situations.
He studied motion by comparing moving power, resistance, distance, and time.
He thought that good character grows through repeated good actions, while good decisions also require experience and prudence.
His writings influenced later scholars, including Thomas Bradwardine and other Oxford thinkers.
summaries.why_it_matters: Kilvington shows that people in the Middle Ages were asking detailed questions about mathematics, motion, decision-making, and knowledge. His work also shows how one method can travel between subjects: logical analysis and measurement were used not only for nature but also for ethics and theology. Studying him helps us see that the history of science and philosophy includes many thinkers who tested older ideas instead of simply repeating them.

important_terms.definition: A careful way of thinking about what is true, using reasons and rules.
The study of nature, change, motion, and physical things.
A skill for making good choices in particular situations, learned through experience.
A case someone imagines to see what would follow, even if it does not happen in real life.
Something without an ending, such as endlessly dividing a line into smaller parts.

questions_to_think_about: Why might imagining an unusual situation help someone test an idea?
Can a person know rules about being good but still make a poor choice? Why?
What would make a moving object go faster or slower?
Can a line really be divided into endlessly smaller parts?

summaries.example: Suppose a mover has force F and an object offers resistance R. Kilvington argues that motion begins whenever F is even slightly greater than R, rather than only when the difference is large. He then examines how the ratio between F and R should determine speed. His analysis challenges a simple reading of Aristotelian motion and uses operations on proportions associated with Euclid and Archimedes.
summaries.summary: Richard Kilvington was an Oxford master and theologian of the fourteenth century and an early member of the Oxford Calculators. His surviving works arose mainly from university lectures and address selected questions rather than following every topic in Aristotle’s works. Kilvington’s distinctive approach combines terminist logic, analysis of limits and degrees, mathematical treatment of proportions, and hypothetical reasoning. In the Sophismata, a disputed sentence is tested by a structured case and arguments for and against it. Such cases can concern observable change or situations that are not physically possible but are logically coherent. In natural philosophy, Kilvington examines how active and resisting capacities produce motion, how speed relates to force and resistance, and how distance and time describe motion. His revised proportional analysis challenges some Aristotelian and Averroist rules, while still working largely within an Aristotelian framework. He also defends an account of continua containing infinitely many proportional parts and distinguishes equality by number of parts from equality by magnitude or quality. In ethics, virtues and vices are changeable qualities with degrees of intensity. Repeated good actions strengthen virtue, but general moral knowledge does not guarantee good conduct. Prudence depends on experience and guides free choice. In theology, Kilvington applies these analytical tools to divine power and knowledge, future contingents, human freedom, grace, sin, and predestination. His views combine Scotist and Ockhamist elements. Later English and continental scholars drew on his logical, physical, ethical, and theological work, especially his analysis of motion.
key_ideas: Kilvington’s work joins terminist logic, mathematical accounts of motion, and theological analysis; methods developed in one field are applied in others.
His Sophismata treats disputed sentences involving alteration, motion, infinity, and knowledge. Hypothetical cases can expose weaknesses in accepted theories without being physically actual.
He accepts an Ockhamist account of continua as containing infinitely many proportional parts, while distinguishing different senses in which infinite sets may be equal or unequal.

In natural philosophy, he analyzes motion through force, resistance, distance, time, limits, and proportions. His rule allows motion whenever force exceeds resistance by any amount and avoids some problems involving very slow motion.
In ethics, virtues and vices can vary in intensity through actions. General moral knowledge is insufficient by itself; prudence requires experience and helps the will make good choices.

In theology, he follows and develops themes associated especially with Duns Scotus while also showing affinities with Ockham. He treats divine power, foreknowledge, contingency, free will, and predestination as connected problems.
summaries.why_it_matters: Kilvington is important for the history of philosophy because he illustrates the close relationship among medieval logic, natural philosophy, mathematics, ethics, and theology. His use of hypothetical cases anticipates a style of reasoning in which a theory is tested by asking what would follow under carefully controlled assumptions. His work on proportions, limits, continuity, and motion contributed to the intellectual setting from which later Oxford theories of motion developed. His ethics also presents a nuanced account of moral development: correct principles matter, but experienced judgment and trained habits matter too.

important_terms.definition: A medieval method in which a disputed statement is examined through a case, arguments on both sides, a resolution, and replies to objections.
A theory of natural change that uses numerical or proportional reasoning to describe motion and related processes.
A capacity to act or to resist being acted upon; Kilvington analyzes motion through the relation between these capacities.
A boundary of a continuous range, such as the greatest or least value reached or approached in a process.
The view that many distinctions used in description—such as time, motion, or degree—are conceptual tools rather than independent things in reality.
An analysis based on a hypothetical situation, used when the situation is logically possible even if it is not physically observed.
The practical ability to choose well in particular circumstances, developed through experience as well as general knowledge.
A distinction between God’s power to act within the established order and power to do anything non-contradictory.

questions_to_think_about: What is gained, and what is lost, when a philosopher studies an impossible or unobservable case?
Why might a theory of speed need more than simply multiplying the ratio of force to resistance?
How does Kilvington distinguish general moral knowledge from the experience needed for prudence?
If future events are contingent, how can a theory explain divine knowledge of them?
Does using the same logical or mathematical method in physics, ethics, and theology strengthen the method, or risk confusing different subjects?

summaries.example: Suppose two students are carrying the same heavy box. If one student pushes harder while the box’s resistance stays the same, the box may move faster. Kilvington would ask how the relationship between pushing power and resistance should be measured. He might also imagine the box moving in an empty space—not because he had observed that, but because an imagined case could reveal whether a rule was consistent.
summaries.summary: Richard Kilvington was a scholar at Oxford during the early 1300s. He later became a theologian and an important church official, but most of his known philosophical writings began as university lectures. He belonged to the first generation of the Oxford Calculators, scholars who made unusually strong use of mathematics in studying motion and change. Kilvington’s only work devoted mainly to logic is the Sophismata. A sophism is a disputed statement examined through a carefully described case, arguments on both sides, and a final resolution. His cases could involve ordinary physical changes, such as becoming whiter, or hypothetical situations that could not be observed but were still logically possible. In natural philosophy, he studied how force and resistance produce motion. He analyzed limits, degrees, speed, distance, and time, and he argued that even a small excess of force over resistance can produce motion. His mathematical treatment of proportions helped make motion easier to describe and influenced Thomas Bradwardine. Kilvington also examined infinity, including the idea that a continuous line contains endlessly many proportional parts. In ethics, he treated virtues and vices as qualities that can become stronger or weaker. Repeated good actions can build virtue, while repeated bad actions can weaken it. Yet general knowledge about morality is not enough for good conduct. Prudence—the ability to judge particular situations well—depends importantly on experience. In theology, Kilvington used logic to discuss God’s power, knowledge of future events, human free will, and predestination. key_ideas: Kilvington used logical and mathematical methods to investigate nature, ethical qualities, and theological questions.
He tested both observed events and hypothetical cases, as long as the cases did not contain a formal contradiction.
His work on motion compared active power with resistance and examined speed through proportions, distance, and time.
He held that virtues and vices can grow stronger or weaker through actions, so moral character changes over time.
He distinguished knowing general moral rules from having the experience needed to choose well in a particular case.
His arguments influenced later Oxford scholars and especially Thomas Bradwardine’s work on motion.
summaries.why_it_matters: Kilvington helps us understand how medieval philosophy could be analytical and mathematical. He did not treat logic as useful only for word puzzles. He applied it to motion, infinity, moral development, and theology. His work also shows that a person can respect an older framework, such as Aristotle’s natural philosophy, while revising parts that seem inconsistent. His account of prudence remains a useful way to think about the difference between memorizing a principle and applying it wisely.

important_terms.definition: A statement or puzzle whose truth is questioned and tested by giving a situation, reasons for and against, and a solution.
The study of nature, including change, bodies, motion, time, and speed.
A hypothetical situation used to explore what would follow from a rule.
The idea that something can have more or less of a quality, such as heat, whiteness, courage, or generosity.
A boundary that helps identify when a capacity or changing quality begins, ends, or reaches a limit.
Endlessness; Kilvington discussed whether a continuum, such as a line, contains endlessly many proportional parts.
The practiced ability to make good decisions in particular situations, especially through experience.

questions_to_think_about: Why could a made-up situation be useful in a serious argument?
Is knowing a rule like “be fair” enough to make a fair decision?
How might resistance affect the speed of an object?
What different meanings might people give to the word “infinite”?
Why might a philosopher study logic before discussing difficult questions about nature or ethics?
